title: Scripting Reproduction Through Platforms: How Chinese Pregnancy Apps Construct Maternal and Paternal Identities
text_snippet: Scripting Reproduction Through Platforms: How Chinese Pregnancy Apps Construct Maternal and Paternal Identities Abstract Pregnancy apps are increasingly embedded in everyday reproductive health, yet their roles in constructing maternal and paternal identities remains underexplored. This study examined how Chinese pregnancy apps produced gendered parental subject positions through algorithmically curated homepage recommendations and app-generated prompts. To conceptualize this process, we developed the concept of platformed reproductive scripts to capture how apps guide users to understand and perform conception, pregnancy, fetal care, and anticipated parenthood. Five Chinese apps were selected using the systematic review-informed method and analyzed through the walkthrough method. Ten simulated accounts with matched expectant mother and expectant father profiles were created to compare role-specific content across the reproductive journey. Thematic analysis showed that the apps celebrated men’s contribution to conception while assigning women more sustained preconception work. title: The Double-Edged Power of Mentors: How Daily Feelings of Power Shape Mentees’ Experiences of Gender- and Race-Based Harm and Support
text_snippet: The Double-Edged Power of Mentors: How Daily Feelings of Power Shape Mentees’ Experiences of Gender- and Race-Based Harm and Support Abstract Power asymmetries shape everyday mistreatment in workplaces and academic training settings, yet little is known about how mentors' momentary feelings of power affect mentees' daily gender- and race-based experiences in real time. Drawing on power-approach and power-amplification theories, we propose that mentors' daily felt power simultaneously energizes sexy-powerful and responsibility-focused feelings and moral crediting beliefs that shape mentees' experiences of sexual harassment, racial mistreatment, and incivility (collectively, HARM) and allyship. In Study 1 of 100 working adults, we validated a brief daily measure of power and found that it activated sexy-powerful and communal feelings, which showed opposing links to sexual harassment intentions. In Study 2, daily surveys from 202 mentor–mentee dyads over 10 days showed that mentors' daily power increased sexy-powerful feelings, communal feelings, and moral crediting beliefs. Contrary to predictions, sexy-powerful feelings predicted lower HARM to mentees, whereas communal feelings and moral crediting beliefs predicted higher incivility—a key component of HARM; moral crediting beliefs also predicted greater allyship.

title: Exploring the Orgasm Gap in Heterosexual Sex: A Swiss and European Online Survey
text_snippet: Exploring the Orgasm Gap in Heterosexual Sex: A Swiss and European Online Survey Abstract The orgasm gap refers to the phenomenon whereby cisgender women experience orgasm less frequently and less reliably than do cisgender men during heterosex. Our study reassesses the orgasm gap in a sample of 2,272 cisgender heterosexual participants from Switzerland and the EU and investigates contributing factors (i.e., social aspects, personal aspects, relationship context, sexual behaviors). In partnersex, we find a large gap of 37.9%, whereas the gap in masturbation is only 3.1%. We also identify an orgasm satisfaction gap, which indicates that women are 26.8% less satisfied than men with their orgasm frequency. While anatomical knowledge is positively associated with orgasm in masturbation, it had no effect in partnersex. Factors such as age, higher sex frequency, stronger sexual desire, committed relationships, open communication, and clitoral-focused practices increase the orgasm frequency for women during heterosex; however, only 9.6% of women report experiencing orgasm from penile-vaginal penetration alone. title: The Kavanaugh Hearings and the #MeToo Movement Through the Distorted Mirror of The Red Pill and Incel Message Boards
text_snippet: The Kavanaugh Hearings and the #MeToo Movement Through the Distorted Mirror of The Red Pill and Incel Message Boards Abstract The “manosphere” is a collection of internet communities across message boards, blogs, and websites where men openly voice their hatred of feminism and veneration of hegemonic masculinity. We explored how two of these communities (Red Pill and Incel) understood and responded to the U.S. Senate hearings on Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, as well as the recently culturally relevant #MeToo movement. Through a reflexive thematic analysis of 98 posts (266,435 words) from Red Pill and Incel, we found that men in these communities tended to construct sexual assault and larger cultural conversations through a worldview that endorses rape myths as true. Victims of sexual assault were viewed as hungry for power. Men (including Kavanaugh) were understood as the real victims of the #MeToo movement. Responses to these constructions of the Kavanaugh hearing and the #MeToo movement included antipathy toward women, hopelessness (Incel), protecting oneself from supposed false sexual assault allegations (Red Pill), and political mobilization attempts. title: Gendered Profiles of Classism Toward People in Poverty: Hostile and Paternalistic Manifestations
text_snippet: Gendered Profiles of Classism Toward People in Poverty: Hostile and Paternalistic Manifestations Abstract Ambivalent classist representations shape support for poverty eradication strategies, yet little is known about how these attitudes differ when directed toward women versus men. We address this gap by conducting latent profile analyses to examine the emergence and prevalence of gendered ambivalent classism profiles across five countries ( N = 4,116; Spain, Argentina, Colombia, Chile, and Mexico). Results revealed a consistent range of classism profiles based on hostile and protective paternalistic attitudes toward women and men, including three ambivalent classist profiles (low, moderate, and high), a high generalized classist profile, a low-classist profile, and a paternalist profile. Profile emergence and prevalence varied by country and by the gender of the target. General trends emerged whereby participants were more likely to belong to paternalistic profiles when evaluating women in poverty compared to men in poverty. Further, those perceiving greater gender and economic inequality, and those identifying as feminists, were more likely to be members of low-classist or paternalistic profiles. title: Zeroes in a Zero-Sum Game: A Netnographic Analysis of Incels’ Construction of Inequality in the Manosphere
text_snippet: Zeroes in a Zero-Sum Game: A Netnographic Analysis of Incels’ Construction of Inequality in the Manosphere Abstract In the Manosphere, a digital space hostile to women, men are depicted as victims of women’s gains. The belief that women’s advancements come at the expense of men is a product of a zero-sum worldview, which posits that one group’s success comes at a cost to others. Importantly, research on zero-sum ideology tends to focus on power between rather than within groups. This focus overlooks grievances of less-advantaged members of privileged groups, such as men who do not receive full benefits of masculine privilege. In this analysis, we examine the ways incels (i.e., involuntary celibates) construct inequality in a presumed zero-sum game. Through a netnography of incels.is, we find that users cast inceldom as a disability and marginalized sexual identity, calling for an uprising to secure reparations for the denial of masculine privilege they believe they are owed (e.g., women’s sexual attention). title: Paternal Affection, Masculinity, and Fathers’ Parenting Self-Efficacy: Findings From an Australian Cohort Study
text_snippet: Paternal Affection, Masculinity, and Fathers’ Parenting Self-Efficacy: Findings From an Australian Cohort Study Abstract Parenting self-efficacy refers to the confidence that parents have in their ability to successfully promote children’s development and to overcome parenting challenges. Yet how parenting self-efficacy unfolds in men remains largely unknown. Developmental ecological models of fathering suggest that fathers’ parenting beliefs, such as parenting self-efficacy, develop through a complex interaction of factors. In the present study, we examine two important individual factors that may influence parenting self-efficacy: men’s recollection of affection received from their own father and men’s cultural values regarding traditional masculinity. Data were obtained from the Australian Longitudinal Study on Male Health (Ten to Men), Wave 1 and Wave 2 of the adult age group ( N = 7,901). After adjustment for covariates and prior depression, we found that higher levels of recalled paternal affection were significantly associated with greater parenting self-efficacy. title: Associations Between Sexual Coercion and Desire Among Women Partnered with Men: The Role of Sexual Coercion Frequency, Type, and Relationship Length
text_snippet: Associations Between Sexual Coercion and Desire Among Women Partnered with Men: The Role of Sexual Coercion Frequency, Type, and Relationship Length Abstract Low sexual desire is a common concern reported by women in committed relationships with men. Low desire is often perceived as a biological issue within women’s bodies; however, the heteronormativity theory of low sexual desire in women partnered with men proposes that it stems from how gender norms shape sexual and romantic relationships. In line with this theory, the current study examined associations between sexual coercion (i.e., using psychological or physical pressure or threats to obtain sex) and desire among a sample of 174 cisgender and gender/sex minority women partnered with men. Using cross-sectional survey data, we tested whether frequency of sexual coercion from a partner and/or the types of sexual coercion used predicted general and recent (across the past four weeks) sexual desire, examining relationship length as a moderator. Generally, results showed that greater sexual coercion frequency was associated with significantly lower general and recent desire, and the strength of this association increased with relationship length. title: Fake Content, Harmful Emotions: The Influence of Being a Victim-Survivor of Sexualised Deepfakes on Women’s Aversive Emotions and Desire for Legal Action
text_snippet: Fake Content, Harmful Emotions: The Influence of Being a Victim-Survivor of Sexualised Deepfakes on Women’s Aversive Emotions and Desire for Legal Action Abstract Sexualised deepfakes involve using artificial intelligence to create fake sexually explicit material of an individual. Across three experimental studies, we tested the psychological impact of sexualised deepfakes on women. Studies 1 ( N = 65) and 2 ( N = 60) asked participants to rate their feelings of objectification and emotions towards being the victim-survivor of sexualised deepfakes, revenge pornography or a non-sexual control condition. In both studies, feelings of objectification and the emotions were higher in the sexualised deepfake and revenge pornography conditions than the control condition. No reliable significant differences in objectification and emotions between the sexualised deepfake and revenge pornography conditions were found. In Study 3 ( N = 626), women were randomly allocated to imagine themselves being the victim-survivor of a non-sexualised deepfake video (control condition), a non-nude deepfake video of them describing a sexual experience (non-nude sexual condition) or a nude deepfake video (nude sexual condition). title: Pervasive Ambiguity About Gender: Quantifying the Cognitive and Affect Experience of Disorientation Related to Changing Understandings of Gender in Society
text_snippet: Pervasive Ambiguity About Gender: Quantifying the Cognitive and Affect Experience of Disorientation Related to Changing Understandings of Gender in Society Abstract This article introduces the concept of pervasive ambiguity about gender to illuminate how individuals experience the destabilization of gender norms in contemporary society. Specifically, it considers how the increasing visibility of transgender and nonbinary identities, alongside broader transformations in the social organization of gender, have unsettled once-stable gender schemas. For many people, this change has produced a sense of pervasive ambiguity—an affective and cognitive experience of disorientation in which individuals struggle to interpret gendered meanings, locate themselves in gendered contexts, and resolve fundamental questions about identity and social norms. Building on Durkheim’s theory of anomie and Ball-Rokeach’s concept of pervasive social ambiguity, this article theorizes pervasive ambiguity about gender as a transitional, situational experience of sociocultural flux. It then operationalizes the concept through the development and validation of the Pervasive Ambiguity About Gender (PAAG) scale in a pair of studies conducted among adults in the U.S. The first study ( N = 491) uses exploratory factor analysis to derive a reliable, nine-item scale. title: A Mile in Her Heels: Do Men and Women Agree on How Often Women Are Sexually Objectified?
text_snippet: A Mile in Her Heels: Do Men and Women Agree on How Often Women Are Sexually Objectified? Abstract Despite extensive research on women’s experiences of sexual objectification, no research has examined whether women and men are aligned in their estimates of how often women have these experiences. Across three studies (one preregistered), we examined discrepancies between how often women reported experiencing sexual objectification and how often men believed women experienced this type of sexual objectification. Participants estimated frequency using a verbally anchored response scale (“ never ” to “ almost always ”) and a numeric count (e.g., times per week). In Studies 1 and 2, men’s estimates of how often women experience sexual objectification were significantly higher than women’s reports. In Studies 2 and 3, women’s estimates for how often the “average young woman” experiences sexual objectification were significantly higher than men’s estimates for overt sexual objectification (e.g., catcalling), but significantly lower than men’s estimates for covert sexual objectification (e.g., leering). title: The “Perfect” Target: Investigating How Target Expectations Shape Perceptions of Gender Harassment
text_snippet: The “Perfect” Target: Investigating How Target Expectations Shape Perceptions of Gender Harassment Abstract Gender harassment, the most prevalent form of sexual harassment, remains notably difficult to recognize in workplace settings. This experimental scenario-based study examined whether the extent to which a target aligns with people's expectations of a “typical” sexual harassment target (i.e., target prototypicality) influences recognition of gender harassment as a type of sexual harassment. Using a repeated-measures two-group design with 132 employed Australian university students, the findings revealed that target prototypicality did not improve identification of gender harassment as sexual harassment. However, target prototypicality significantly influenced perceptions of the target, perpetrator, and organization. Together, these findings highlight the need for organizations and practitioners to both improve recognition of gender harassment and address prescriptive expectations surrounding target responses.

title: Reading the Room: How Workers Perceive Organizational Climate Toward Sexual Harassment
text_snippet: Reading the Room: How Workers Perceive Organizational Climate Toward Sexual Harassment Abstract Research identifies an organization’s climate toward sexual harassment as the strongest predictor of sexual harassment prevalence. Yet how employees come to perceive their organization’s climate toward sexual harassment has not been explored. Drawing on data from 35 interviews with restaurant workers in Madison, Wisconsin, we show that workers overwhelmingly draw from their experiences and interactions in the workplace, rather than written organizational policies, to make sense of the organization’s climate toward sexual harassment. Workers who perceived their organization to be intolerant of unwanted sexual or sexist behavior described witnessing disrespectful or harassing behaviors being preempted, interrupted, or addressed. However, workers who did experience unwanted sexual or sexist behaviors rarely concluded that their organization was broadly tolerant of sexual harassment. Instead, they often drew boundaries, perceiving their organization as more tolerant of such behavior from high-status members of the organization than from others (particularly customers and Latino employees). title: Survivor or Victim: Labels and Crime-Type Interact to Influence Perceiver Impressions of Psychological Pain and Hardship
text_snippet: Survivor or Victim: Labels and Crime-Type Interact to Influence Perceiver Impressions of Psychological Pain and Hardship Abstract Many women are the targets of sexual violence, and while the psychological distress and physical pain experienced by people who have been sexually assaulted are well-documented, less research has used experimental designs to evaluate factors in how perceivers understand the pain and hardship of women who have experienced sexual assault. Furthermore, the labels commonly used for targets of sexual violence (i.e., “victim” and “survivor”) carry differing connotations that could have important implications for how the pain of women who have been sexually assaulted is perceived. We experimentally assessed the influence of labeling in sexual assault and two other crimes (i.e., mugging and identity theft) on perceptions of psychological pain, hardship, and support needed. Interaction effects of crime type and label were observed for hardship, current psychological pain, and sensitivity to psychological pain, indicating that the effects of labels (survivor, victim, person who experienced) on perception vary by crime type. title: Pornography Use and Sexual Well-Being: Exploring Gender Differences Among Mexican Young Adults
text_snippet: Pornography Use and Sexual Well-Being: Exploring Gender Differences Among Mexican Young Adults Abstract Although pornography use has risen globally, research on its psychological and relational correlates remains centered in Western contexts. This exploratory study examines how pornography use relates to sexual beliefs and behaviors among Mexican young adults, expanding prior research into a Latin American context. Utilizing sexual script theory, which highlights the pathways of sexual learning, often highly gendered in nature, we examined whether frequency of pornography use predicted reliance on pornography for arousal, incorporation of pornography into partnered sex, enjoyment of sexual intimacy, and sexual satisfaction. Results indicated that greater pornography use was associated with increased reliance on pornography for arousal, more frequent incorporation into partnered sexual activity, and lower sexual satisfaction, but was not related to enjoyment of sexual intimacy. Due to measurement invariance, analyses were estimated separately for men and women; however, the direction and statistical significance of the structural associations were consistent across gender-specific models. title: Intergenerational Links Between Parents’ and Children’s Hostile and Benevolent Sexism
text_snippet: Intergenerational Links Between Parents’ and Children’s Hostile and Benevolent Sexism Abstract Research has confirmed that adults’ hostile sexism and benevolent sexism harm adult women and men. Yet, men’s and women’s sexist attitudes also shape parenting behavior, and children agree with hostile and benevolent sexism at a young age. Our research connects these emerging insights to test the intergenerational links between parents’ and children’s sexism in 175 family triads: mothers, fathers, and their 8-year-old child (51% girls, 49% boys). Mothers and fathers completed standard measures of hostile and benevolent sexism, and children completed a newly developed task to assess children’s hostile and benevolent gender attitudes. Fathers’ hostile sexism predicted their children’s agreement with hostile gender attitudes, and mothers’ benevolent sexism predicted their children’s benevolent gender attitudes, irrespective of child gender. Additionally, mothers’ hostile sexism predicted their sons’ but not daughters’ hostile gender attitudes. The results remained when including key covariates (e.g., children’s age and theory of mind; parents’ education, employment, and primary caregiver status). title: Discrimination Toward Transgender and Non-Binary People: The Moderating Roles of Political Conservatism and Religiosity in Hiring Decisions
text_snippet: Discrimination Toward Transgender and Non-Binary People: The Moderating Roles of Political Conservatism and Religiosity in Hiring Decisions Abstract Transgender and non-binary (TNB) people experience high rates of discrimination and are at greater risk of poor mental health compared to the general population. However, lacking is experimental evidence pertaining to factors that predict discrimination against TNB people, and the mechanisms underlying these effects. Across two experimental employment evaluation studies ( N = 940), we tested whether TNB job applicants would be rated more negatively than cisgender applicants, and whether these effects were mediated by anticipated liking. We also tested both political conservatism and religiosity as potential moderators. In Study 1 ( N = 375, M age = 37.55 years), those who were more politically conservative viewed applicants as less competent and were less likely to recommend hiring the person when the applicant was TNB rather than cisgender. In Study 2 ( N = 565, M age = 38.84 years), political conservatism (but not religiosity) again moderated the effects of applicant gender status on ratings of competence and hiring recommendation. title: Entitativity Predicts “Counter-Allyship” Towards a Black Woman Complainant of Violent Sexual Harassment Through Elevated Promiscuity Attributions
text_snippet: Entitativity Predicts “Counter-Allyship” Towards a Black Woman Complainant of Violent Sexual Harassment Through Elevated Promiscuity Attributions Abstract Black women in the United States continue to face disproportionate gender-based sexual violence, often compounded by stereotypes that portray them as sexually promiscuous. This study examines how perceptions of entitativity —the belief that Black women form a cohesive, interchangeable group—shape negative reactions toward a Black woman who reports workplace sexual harassment by a White supervisor. Using a sample of White American adults ( N = 197), participants completed measures of right-wing authoritarianism (RWA), perceived Black women’s entitativity, promiscuity attributions, and two forms of “counter-allyship”: blaming the complainant and expressing sympathy toward the perpetrator (“himpathy”). Results showed that perceiving Black women as a highly unified group predicted stronger promiscuity attributions, which, in turn, increased counter-allyship among participants high (but not low) in RWA. These findings reveal how group-based stereotyping processes and authoritarian attitudes intersect to undermine empathy for Black women survivors of workplace harassment. title: Gender Ideologies and Sexual Agency: A Gendered Analysis of Associations Among Heterosexual and LGBQ+ Men, Women, and Nonbinary Emerging Adults
text_snippet: Gender Ideologies and Sexual Agency: A Gendered Analysis of Associations Among Heterosexual and LGBQ+ Men, Women, and Nonbinary Emerging Adults Abstract Sexual agency is recognized as a fundamental dimension of young people’s navigation of both pleasure and protection in their sexual lives. However, sexual agency is difficult to navigate in a social landscape where traditional gender ideologies remain powerful forces in young people’s experiences of sexuality. While prior research has examined how femininity ideologies constrain girls and women and masculinity ideologies constrain boys and men, studies have not investigated how femininity and masculinity may both work to shape sexual agency. Research on these relationships has further left unexplored sexual and gender minority individuals’ experiences. I explore the implications of femininity and masculinity ideologies and their interaction for sexual agency in service of pleasure (asking for what one wants sexually) and protection (saying no to unwanted sex and using contraception), for a sample of heterosexual and LGBQ+ women, men, and nonbinary emerging adults. title: Prioritizing Work or Family? Investigating Women’s and Men’s Work-Family Decisions
text_snippet: Prioritizing Work or Family? Investigating Women’s and Men’s Work-Family Decisions Abstract Despite societal change, women and men still differ in the extent to which they prioritize work and family. Women more often reduce work hours or adjust careers to prioritize family needs, whereas men more often work overtime or decline family responsibilities to advance their careers. This study tested two possible explanations, that women and men differ in (1) how they perceive the costs and benefits of prioritizing work versus family; and (2) how they weigh these costs and benefits when deciding which domain to prioritize. We presented 625 employed participants (309 women, 316 men) with six scenarios involving work-family trade-offs. Analyses confirmed that women were more willing than men to prioritize family over work and less willing to prioritize work over family, even though both women and men were generally more willing to prioritize family. Women’s greater willingness to prioritize family was partially explained by higher perceived family benefits, and men’s greater willingness to prioritize work by lower perceived family costs. title: Measuring Mankeeping: Development and Validation of a Scale Assessing How Women Experience the Impact of Men's Declining Social Networks
text_snippet: Measuring Mankeeping: Development and Validation of a Scale Assessing How Women Experience the Impact of Men's Declining Social Networks Abstract Mankeeping was theorized as the unreciprocated labor women take on to compensate for losses in men’s social networks, thereby reducing the burden on families, heterosexual bonds, and men. However, there is currently no validated instrument that can reliably assess this theory. Across two studies, this paper aimed to develop and validate a scale to evaluate women’s experiences of mankeeping . Study 1 describes the scale development process using data derived from 402 heterosexually partnered women residing in the United States. Exploratory factor analysis showed a six-factor solution for a 46-item instrument, titled the Mankeeping Scale – Partner Report (MSPR), which demonstrated good reliability and validity. Study 2 tested the initial factor structure and measurement invariance of the MSPR in a sample of women in the United Kingdom ( N = 395). Confirmatory factor analyses revealed the original six-factor model provides the best model fit. Results provide strong evidence for the configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance of the MSPR across both countries. title: Sexual Communication Self-Efficacy and Sexual Victimization Risk Among College Women Who Use Alcohol
text_snippet: Sexual Communication Self-Efficacy and Sexual Victimization Risk Among College Women Who Use Alcohol Abstract Gendered sexual norms and power dynamics shape women’s ability to communicate sexual boundaries and negotiate consent, particularly within alcohol-involved contexts. Sexual communication self-efficacy is often conceptualized as an individual skill; however, it may reflect broader gendered constraints that influence sexual victimization risk. The current study investigated the association between sexual communication self-efficacy and sexual victimization frequency and severity among college women who drink. Participants were 199 cisgender, sexually active college women who completed self-reported measures of sexual communication self-efficacy, past-year alcohol use (AUDIT-C), and sexual victimization experiences as part of an experimental study on sexual refusal assertiveness among college women. Results indicated that lower sexual communication self-efficacy was associated with a higher frequency and severity of sexual victimization after controlling for age. title: Man Up? How Men and Women Respond to Ads Portraying Men in Gender Counter-Stereotypical Roles
text_snippet: Man Up? How Men and Women Respond to Ads Portraying Men in Gender Counter-Stereotypical Roles Abstract The negative effects of gender stereotypes have led many communication professionals to adopt strategies aimed at challenging them. One of these is counter-stereotypical advertising (CSA), based on representing men and women in non-traditional gender roles. However, little is still known about the actual effects of CSA and whether it truly leads to the intended outcomes. This study aims to examine these effects by focusing on CSA portraying men in domestic roles. In a two-wave repeated-measures experimental study ( N = 254), we examined how different types of domestic CSA affected people’s views about traditional gender roles. Participants were divided in three groups and exposed to different types of ads: CSA showing only men domestic roles, CSA showing men in domestic roles and women in counter-stereotypical roles, or control ads. Results showed that women who saw ads with counter-stereotypical roles became less traditional in their gender role beliefs, compared to women in the control group. title: Escaping Transgender Stigma: Differentiating Gender Identity Concealment From Assigned Sex Concealment
text_snippet: Escaping Transgender Stigma: Differentiating Gender Identity Concealment From Assigned Sex Concealment Abstract Many gender minorities conceal their identity to escape structural and social stigma and protect their own mental health, yet their concealment strategies remain poorly understood. We argue that gender identity concealment and assigned sex concealment represent discrete concealment pathways with distinct mechanisms and consequences. A convenience sample of 185 transgender and gender diverse Australian adults completed an online survey exploring gender identity concealment and assigned sex concealment. Scores representing active concealment and disclosure were calculated for each concealment pathway. Score distributions and discriminant validity statistics confirmed that gender identity concealment and assigned sex concealment were neither interchangeable nor mutually exclusive. gender identity concealment was associated with decreased social support and assigned sex concealment with increased discrimination. Only gender identity concealment was related to depression—participants who did not attempt to conceal their gender identity at all were significantly less depressed than those who did. title: Masculinity, Not Femininity, is Associated with Sexual Desirability Among Grindr Users in Australia
text_snippet: Masculinity, Not Femininity, is Associated with Sexual Desirability Among Grindr Users in Australia Abstract Whether men who have sex with men see themselves as sexy is influenced by their gender expression – that is, by their performance of masculinity and femininity. Generally, while masculine men attract others’ sexual interest, feminine men are relegated to the sexual margins. Hegemonic masculinity underpins the disproportionate value gay communities place in masculinity over femininity. Yet norms of gender expression and sexual desirability also vary between gay subcultures. Here, we tested the relationships between sexually desirability, masculinity, and femininity, and whether these relationships were moderated by participants’ membership in a gay subculture. Using dynamic structural equation modelling, we analyzed experience sampling data from 234 Grindr users ( T = 12,162) collected in May 2022. We found that masculinity, but not femininity, was associated with how sexually desirable Grindr users felt, but only limited evidence that these relationships differed between subcultures. title: (Re)Imagining Motherhood Among Young Women: Between Neoliberal Subjection and Feminist Emancipation in a Familistic Context
text_snippet: (Re)Imagining Motherhood Among Young Women: Between Neoliberal Subjection and Feminist Emancipation in a Familistic Context Abstract This article examines how neoliberal subjectivity has been established in young women who are activists in feminist spaces and social reproduction struggles in Barcelona. Based on interviews with 19 white, cisgender, non-mother women—highly educated but living in precarious conditions—who actively participate in these movements, the study explores how neoliberal logic shapes their perceptions of motherhood. Neoliberal subjectivity, understood as a cost-benefit calculation prioritizing self-optimization, pressures women to balance motherhood and careers as individual responsibilities without state support. This logic often influences middle- or upper-class women aligned with neoliberal feminism. However, our findings reveal that participants frequently reject traditional maternity or consider remaining childless rather than adopting the neoliberal multifaceted woman model.
